target.title: fix: restore terminal pgrp after PATH lookup
target.body:
## Summary
- Restore the terminal foreground process group after the shell PATH probe in `ShellCommandLocator.runShellCommand`, so `watch` sessions keep TTY foreground ownership and `Ctrl+C` keeps working after CLI commands.
- The restore blocks `SIGTTOU` on the calling thread across `tcsetpgrp`. It runs from a background process group — the interactive probe shell moves the terminal foreground and the post-completion `kill(-pgid, SIGTERM)` cleanup strands it on a now-dead group — where the default `SIGTTOU` action would otherwise stop the CLI.

## Validation
- `swift build --product CodexBarCLI -c debug` — passes (branch rebased onto current `main`).
- Deterministic PTY reproduction under a real controlling terminal (harness + transcript in the review comment), across three restore variants:
  - **no restore** (pre-fix `main`): terminal foreground left stranded on a dead process group → the hang.
  - **bare `tcsetpgrp`**: process **stopped by `SIGTTOU`**, foreground still not restored.
  - **`SIGTTOU`-blocked `tcsetpgrp`** (this PR): foreground cleanly restored, no stop.

target.title: fix(workboard): resolve parent dependency status via targeted lookups, not a full-corpus scan
target.body:
### Problem

`WorkboardStore.dependencyTargetStatus()` (`extensions/workboard/src/store.ts`)
checks whether a card's parent(s) are `done` before promoting it out of a
dependency-held status. To do that, it called the fully **unscoped**
`this.list()` — every card, on every board, fully materialized via
`entries()` + `readCard()` — and built a `Map` from it, just to look up 1-2
parent ids.

`dispatch()` calls `promoteDependencyReady()` (which calls
`dependencyTargetStatus()`) once per card in its board-scoped dispatch pass.
So every parented card being checked in a single dispatch pass re-paid for a
full-corpus re-scan: **O(parented_cards_in_pass × total_corpus_size ×
queries_per_card)**. `readCard()` alone issues 4 separate synchronous SQL
statements per row (metadata, events, child rows, labels), so on a
multi-thousand-row corpus this is thousands of synchronous SQL round-trips
per dispatch pass, once per parented card.

### How this was found

Root-caused via a live CDP CPU profile of a real, reproducible
`openclaw workboard dispatch --board <board>` call that was taking 160s+
wall-clock on a corpus of ~5770 cards, despite the dispatch handler's own
instrumented pass timers reporting well under 1 second. Attached Node's
inspector (`--inspect`) to the already-running gateway process, used
`Profiler.start`/`Profiler.stop` over the CDP protocol scoped exactly around
a real reproduction of the stall (161.8s elapsed, matching the known
symptom), and analyzed the resulting `.cpuprofile`.

**93.3% of the profiled wall-clock time** (142s self-time in a native `all()`
binding + 8.7s in `prepare()`, out of 162s total) was attributed to one call
chain:

```
dispatch()
  -> promoteDependencyReady()
    -> dependencyTargetStatus()
      -> list()
        -> entries()
          -> readCard()  (4 sync SQL statements per row)
```

This ruled out the leading working theory for this class of symptom (generic
Node event-loop starvation from a concurrent embedded/CLI agent session
monopolizing the process, as tracked in #84903 / #101895) — for this
specific, reproducible stall, the entire cost is inside the dispatch call's
own synchronous execution, not contention with unrelated work. The call
stack's `runMicrotasks → processTicksAndRejections → (root)` frames above the
hot path are simply how V8's CPU profiler represents async/await
continuations between awaited promises; they are not evidence of a different
concurrent job running.

### Fix

Replace the unscoped `list()` + `Map` lookup with targeted `get(parentId)`
calls — `get()` is already a single indexed-row lookup
(`this.store.lookup(id)`) used everywhere else in this file:

```ts
// before
const cards = new Map((await this.list()).map((entry) => [entry.id, entry]));
const parentsDone = parents.every((parentId) => cards.get(parentId)?.status === "done");

// after
const parentCards = await Promise.all(parents.map((parentId) => this.get(parentId)));
const parentsDone = parentCards.every((parent) => parent?.status === "done");
```

Complexity drops from O(total corpus size) to O(`parents.length`) — normally
1, since `cardParentIds()` already dedupes. Behavior is unchanged:
`parent?.status === "done"` on the `get()` result is exactly what
`cards.get(parentId)?.status === "done"` computed from the unscoped `list()`
Map for both the found and not-found (`undefined`) cases.

### Testing

- New regression test in `store.test.ts`
  (`"resolves parent dependency status with targeted lookups instead of a
  full-corpus scan"`): creates 1 parent + 8 children with `parents: [parent.id]`,
  spies on the underlying keyed store's `entries()`, completes the parent, runs
  `dispatch()`, and asserts:
  - all 8 children are promoted to `ready` (functional correctness, unchanged
    from before the fix)
  - `entries()` is called **at most once** during the dispatch pass — before
    the fix this would have been 9 calls (1 outer board-scoped `list()` + 1
    inner unscoped `list()` per parented card being checked)
- Full extension suite: **113/113 pass**
  (`npx vitest run extensions/workboard/src/`)

### Scope note

`dependsOn()` (same file) has an identical unscoped-`list()` pattern, used
only for cycle-detection at parent/child link-creation time — not on the
dispatch hot path, and there's no profiling evidence it's ever expensive in
practice (link creation is comparatively rare). Deliberately left out of this
PR to keep the change matched 1:1 to the measured problem; worth a follow-up
if it's ever shown to be hot.

### Relationship to #101895 / #84903

#101895 was our earlier report of this exact symptom (`workboard.cards.dispatch`
taking 250s+ wall-clock), which was auto-triaged as a duplicate and merged into
#84903 (generic event-loop-starvation tracker) under the theory that a
concurrent embedded/CLI agent session was starving the gateway's single event
loop. The live CPU profile above shows that, for this specific stall, that
theory doesn't hold — the cost is entirely inside `dispatch()`'s own
synchronous execution. Leaving a comment on both issues linking back to this
PR; the general event-loop-starvation question tracked in #84903 may still be
real for other symptoms, but this particular reproduction is fully explained
and fixed by the change here.

Verified locally against a real corpus (~5770 Workboard cards): the exact
`workboard.cards.dispatch` RPC call that took 160-163s wall-clock before this
fix consistently completed in **2.9s** after, with internal pass-timer
instrumentation showing the fix itself added no measurable overhead
(<1ms, consistent with pre-fix internal timings).


### Real behavior proof

Redacted excerpt from the deployed instance's own gateway log, straight from
`journalctl`, showing repeated real `workboard.cards.dispatch` RPC calls
against a live board with a ~5,770-card corpus, immediately before and after
this fix was deployed (connection/request IDs already truncated by the
logger itself; nothing else redacted):

**Before** (unscoped `list()` scan on every parented card in the pass):
```
2026-07-11T18:32:44.689Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 159519ms
2026-07-11T18:47:39.256Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 154351ms
2026-07-11T19:02:42.699Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 157688ms
2026-07-11T19:08:04.708Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 159080ms
2026-07-11T19:17:40.639Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 155731ms
2026-07-11T19:25:57.209Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 158484ms
2026-07-11T19:32:41.887Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 157259ms
```

**After** (targeted `get(parentId)` lookups; internal `pass_total`
instrumentation, unrelated to this PR, confirms the fix itself adds no
measurable overhead — consistently under 1 second before and after):
```
2026-07-11T19:43:10.772Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2912ms
2026-07-11T19:45:07.069Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2870ms
2026-07-11T20:00:08.020Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2843ms
2026-07-11T20:15:07.584Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2783ms
2026-07-11T20:30:07.233Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2881ms
2026-07-11T20:45:07.163Z [ws] res workboard.cards.dispatch 2780ms
```

Same recurring dispatch call (a `*/15` cron against the same board/corpus),
same deployment, only the code change in between: 154-160s consistently,
every time, before; 2.7-2.9s consistently, every time, after. ~55x.

The underlying `.cpuprofile` referenced above (CDP `Profiler.start`/`stop`
captured over a live-attached inspector, 645,052 samples, 161.8s elapsed)
is not attached directly, since it's a full capture of a real, large
production Workboard corpus — chrome://inspect-format CPU profiles record
call-stack frames (function name/file/line), not card contents, but the
file/module paths and process metadata in it are unredacted and it's large
(5.4MB) enough that hand-redacting isn't practical. The self-time breakdown
already summarized above (93.3% in `all()`/`prepare()` under
`dependencyTargetStatus() -> list() -> entries() -> readCard()`) is the
finding taken directly from analyzing that profile; happy to produce a
sanitized frame-only summary if a maintainer wants to inspect it further.

target.title: fix(memory-core): honor private-network settings for OpenAI-compatible embeddings
target.body:
## Summary

- Rebases PR #94344 onto current main and resolves the OpenAI-compatible embedding provider conflicts without changing the intended SSRF contract.
- Updates the added SSRF tests to match the exported `LookupFn` overload shape.
- Updates the memory config docs to describe exact configured `baseUrl` origin trust (`scheme://host:port`) without widening trust across protocols or ports.
- Prevents configured local-service acquisition and health probes when the selected provider explicitly sets `request.allowPrivateNetwork: false`.
- **Why it matters / User impact:** Operators using configured OpenAI-compatible memory embedding providers need the selected provider's private-endpoint policy to behave predictably: omitted policy preserves exact configured origin compatibility, explicit `false` fails closed, and explicit `true` allows broader private-network access.
- **Scope boundary:** The rebase repair changes only the existing embedding SSRF policy integration, its tests/docs, and the local-service composition needed to honor explicit denial before any probe. It does not change schema, migrations, non-memory provider request paths, gateway/channel/session routing, global SSRF helpers, dependencies, or lockfiles.

Fixes #94166

## Origin / follow-up

N/A — existing PR author repair for #94344.

## Competition / linked PR analysis

- **Linked PR(s):** #94180 (`feat(memory-core): allow private network endpoints for memory embeddings`) and adjacent #96074 (`fix(memory): honor provider request proxy for embeddings`). The public-contract helper also flagged #92307 through an environment/version term, but #92307 is about exec-approval startup warnings and is not the same embedding/private-network contract.
- **Gap in linked PR(s):** #94180 adds a memory-specific config surface, `memorySearch.remote.network.dangerouslyAllowPrivateNetwork`, for a trust decision that the selected model provider can already express with `models.providers.<id>.request.allowPrivateNetwork`.
- **Why this patch is better/canonical:** This PR reuses the existing provider transport-trust contract as the canonical source of truth for configured providers instead of introducing a second memory-only knob. This update only repairs the review findings on that existing approach.
- **Local real behavior proof advantage:** The current-head bounded proof exercises the real `memory status --deep --json` CLI path against a loopback/private OpenAI-compatible daemon backed by the actual FastEmbed `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` model. Omitted policy succeeds through exact-origin trust with one `/v1/embeddings` request, explicit `request.allowPrivateNetwork: false` is blocked before the daemon receives any request, and explicit `true` succeeds with one `/v1/embeddings` request.

target.title: fix(agents): adopt orphaned managed worktrees left by a crash between git worktree add and registry insert
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A gateway crash (OOM kill, forced restart) landing between `git worktree add` and the registry insert inside `ManagedWorktreeService.create()` leaves an on-disk worktree and an `openclaw/<name>` branch that no managed API can ever see, repair, or remove: `list()`/`get()` never show it, every `gc()` pass skips it forever, and any later `create()` with the same name fails hard with `branch already exists`. The only way out today is manual operator surgery (`git worktree remove` + `git branch -D`) outside the managed API. Reported with source-level analysis in #103239; this PR makes the orphan self-heal (gc adopts it; a retried create adopts it and preserves the caller's owner) while leaving foreign/detached worktrees untouched.

## Summary

- Problem: A crash between `git worktree add` and `insertRegistryWorktree()` inside `ManagedWorktreeService.create()` leaves a live git worktree + `openclaw/<name>` branch with no registry row. `reconcileOrphans()` explicitly skips it forever (invisible to `list()`/`gc()`), and a retried `create()` with the same name dead-ends on `branch already exists`.
- Why it matters: In real deployments (OOM kill, forced restart) the orphan is permanently unrecoverable through the managed API — only manual `git worktree remove` + `git branch -D` unblocks the name.
- What changed: recovery happens through the retried `create()` path only. `create()`'s branch-exists guard self-heals the exact crashed-create signature (live worktree at the derived path on exactly `refs/heads/openclaw/<name>`, no registry row) instead of dead-ending: it atomically claims the path in the registry (`insertRegistryWorktreeIfPathFree()`, a single Kysely `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE NOT EXISTS (live row at path)` — no schema change), then re-provisions (`copyIncludedFiles()` + `runSetupScript()`), preserving the caller's `ownerKind`/`ownerId` and recording the real resolved base. Only the claim holder may provision or destroy the path: a losing adopter provably touches nothing, and a holder whose re-provisioning fails removes the worktree and deletes its own row. The registry carries a persisted readiness contract: `readiness ('provisioning'|'ready')` (closed union; additive `ensureColumn` migration per repo precedent — backfill-as-ready is provably safe because no release tag contains the worktrees feature, and unreleased-main builds inserted rows only post-provisioning). The claim inserts `provisioning`; a single UPDATE flips to `ready` only after copy+setup succeed. Every usable-record path is gated on ready (`findLiveByOwner` filters in SQL; the entry shortcut and claim-loser throw a closed `WorktreeProvisioningError`; `restore()` revives as ready; provisioning rows are leases with heartbeats (`lastActiveAt` bumped at claim, post-copy, and at the ready flip): gc reaps only leases SILENT past `PROVISIONING_STALE_MS` — a persisted holder-liveness signal, so claim age alone can never kill a live-but-slow holder — restoring background recovery for auto-named orphans, while a reaped-mid-flight create fails closed with `WorktreeProvisioningReapedError`; a provisioning row whose directory vanished is hard-deleted (branch + row; no snapshot, no user work) so the name stays genuinely retriable). The gateway protocol's `WorktreeRecordSchema` gains an additive optional `readiness` enum (no version bump). Normal (non-adopting) `create()` uses the identical claim-early ordering (claim immediately after `git worktree add`; both paths share one claim → provision-as-holder → holder-only-cleanup helper), establishing the invariant that an in-flight create always holds a live row — so the no-row+live-worktree signature genuinely means a crashed create, and an in-flight worktree can never be adopted, re-provisioned, or destroyed by a concurrent same-name call. Every new live registry row is uniqueness-enforced through the one claim. `reconcileOrphans()`/gc remains preserve-only (upstream behavior) — background adoption is deliberately not shipped (see Risks). `git.ts` additively parses the porcelain `branch` field for the adoption signature check.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): gc keeps upstream's preserve-only behavior for foreign/detached and live git-listed worktrees (only dead debris and stale provisioning rows are cleaned); no protocol version bump; no changes to snapshot semantics; web UI status label deliberately unchanged (would pull in i18n regeneration disproportionate to this PR).

## What Problem This Solves

The Control UI mock has limited curated chat state for design QA, so reviewers have to rely on ad hoc sessions when checking empty chat, longer transcripts, markdown rendering, code blocks, tables, warnings, and recoverable error copy.

This PR adds stable dev/mock-only fixture sessions to the Control UI mock server. The proposed fixtures cover a New session empty state, a coding session, a response-shape showcase, and a markdown showcase without changing production gateway or session APIs.

## User Impact

There is no production user-facing behavior change. Developers and designers can load stable mock chat sessions for future Control UI visual review.

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

- The runtime already walks `memory/` recursively via `collectMemoryFilesFromDir` (`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.ts`), so nested files like `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md` are indexed and searched. But several agent-facing descriptors and public docs still said `memory/*.md`, which can mislead agents into thinking the index is flat.
- This PR updates the remaining stale references to `memory/**/*.md`. No runtime behavior change.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance
- `src/config/schema.help.ts` — `agents.defaults.memorySearch` help text
- `docs/concepts/memory-builtin.md`, `memory.md`, `system-prompt.md`
- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/reference/token-use.md`
- `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256` regenerated via `pnpm config:docs:gen`

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

**Real environment tested**: Installed OpenClaw `2026.5.20` (npm global, current `latest` published build, ahead of the `acf265d` base this PR branches from), against the live workspace `~/.openclaw/workspace-moku` used by the gateway. ## Summary

In this PR, the Appearance text-size setting applies across Control UI content typography instead of only affecting the chat transcript. Shared content font sizes now route through `--control-ui-text-scale`, while touch-primary text-entry controls keep the existing 16px minimum so the 90% text-size stop does not reintroduce mobile Safari focus zoom.

## Screenshots

Settings at the default M text size, showing the Appearance text-size control in English.

![Settings text size at M](https://mystic-bonnet-p3d4.here.now/pr-100934-settings-text-size-m-en.png)

Overview at XXL text size, showing the larger page typography across cards and form controls.

![Overview using XXL text size](https://mystic-bonnet-p3d4.here.now/pr-100934-overview-xxl-en.png)

Channels at XXL text size, showing the larger channel cards and actions.

![Channels using XXL text size](https://mystic-bonnet-p3d4.here.now/pr-100934-channels-xxl-en.png)

Mobile Overview at XXL text size, showing the narrow layout with scaled content typography.

![Mobile overview using XXL text size](https://mystic-bonnet-p3d4.here.now/pr-100934-mobile-overview-xxl-en.png)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes the Appearance text-size setting so it affects Control UI content typography beyond the chat transcript. Before this PR, the setting could be saved while many Settings, quick settings, overview, channel, session, skill, and content surfaces still used fixed font sizes.

## Why This Change Was Made

In this PR, shared Control UI font sizes route through the existing `--control-ui-text-scale` value instead of hard-coded pixel sizes. The change keeps layout chrome and spacing stable while letting readable content, forms, cards, chat text, composer text, and page typography respond to S/M/L/XL/XXL.

Touch-primary text-entry controls keep the existing `--control-ui-input-text-size` minimum so the 90% text-size stop does not shrink mobile inputs below 16px and reintroduce Safari focus zoom.

## User Impact

Changing Text size in Appearance now produces visible typography changes across the main product surfaces, while M remains the normal/default size.

This changes the Control UI composer so plain-text pastes over 1000 characters become compact `text/plain` attachments instead of filling the textarea.

Short text pastes still behave like normal textarea input. Image pastes still use the existing image attachment flow.

## Details

- Converts long plain-text paste events into `pasted-text-*.txt` composer attachments.
- Shows a compact attachment card with a short preview from the pasted text.
- Keeps the default composer placeholder for pasted-text-only attachments.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

target.title: Preserve Claude quota state across placeholders
target.body:
## Summary

- treat Claude's synthetic no-session window as a non-authoritative observation for depleted/restored, threshold, and predictive warning state
- keep synthetic session samples out of plan-utilization history and reset events while continuing to evaluate weekly usage
- update the accepted predictive-warning spec to reflect the released default-off Notifications setting and placeholder semantics

Follow-up to #1960. This complements #2060's reset-boundary hardening by handling the explicit Claude placeholder marker before any notification or history state mutates.

## Behavior proof

Before the fix, real -> placeholder -> same-real sequences could emit restored/depleted loops, clear fired thresholds, or re-arm predictive session warnings. The new regressions fail against the unguarded implementation and now prove that:

- depleted, threshold, and predictive state survives a synthetic placeholder
- weekly threshold and predictive evaluation still proceeds during that placeholder
- a genuine reported 0%-used session remains authoritative
- synthetic sessions do not create history points or consume reset detection state

## Validation

- `swift test --filter 'ClaudeSyntheticPlaceholderNotificationTests|RateWindowSyntheticPlaceholderTests|PredictivePaceWarningTests|UsageStoreSessionQuotaTransitionTests|UsageStorePlanUtilizationTests|CodexSessionQuotaFalseRestoreTests'` - 135 tests in 6 suites passed
- `make check` - passed (format, lint, repository, documentation, and locale checks)
- `make test` - the local sharded run reached an unrelated existing `CodexAccountScopedRefreshTests/default dashboard refresh path discards stale completion after account switch` timeout (exit 124); no changed-area assertion failed, and CI remains the clean-environment full-matrix gate
- exact-head CI - all 8 checks passed, including both macOS Swift-test shards, both Linux build/test lanes, lint, the aggregate gate, and GitGuardian

Dependencies are unchanged. Unit validation used isolated stores, notifier spies, and fictitious identities; no live provider or Keychain probes were run.

## Exact-head fixture runtime proof

Exact commit `246d2da5adadfaa6ef49b48b13f0c86239196a48`, debug app executable SHA-256 `368a3c12e8518da6d1eea61dc7df1e4db54a1e44a25eb3cc010ae62072c9b043`:

- launched the actual app process under LLDB with an isolated `CFFIXED_USER_HOME`, config, and `CODEX_HOME`; every provider was disabled, test-mode notification delivery was suppressed, and logs confirmed Keychain access stayed disabled
- drove the real `AppDelegate` `UsageStore` and `SessionQuotaNotifier` through real -> synthetic placeholder -> same-real session observations, with weekly usage changing during the placeholder
- notifier logs contained exactly one each of `quota-warning-claude-session-50`, `predictive-pace-warning-claude-session`, `quota-warning-claude-weekly-50`, `predictive-pace-warning-claude-weekly`, and `session-claude-depleted`; `session-claude-restored` appeared zero times
- post-sequence state retained `session_remaining=0`, session/weekly fired thresholds `[50]`, and one predictive episode key per lane
- the isolated persisted history contained session `[40, 80, 80]` and weekly `[20, 20, 90, 90]`: the synthetic session `0` was absent while the same observation's weekly `90` point was retained

No real credentials, browser cookies, network provider calls, sounds, or on-screen alerts were used.
